title: Day 1 of letting an AI trading agent run a small real account: one share of AMZN and a rule
author: Accomplished_Fun_408
selftext:
Disclosure: I work at Flow AI, the company behind Bobby, an AI trading agent, and RockFlow, the brokerage the account sits at. My own money, small size, under $2K at risk. Not advice, my own calls.

I'm publishing this log from the start. Days 1 to 17 happened between Sept 21 and Oct 7 and come straight from the broker's order export; I'll post them over the next week, then it goes live.

Setup: Bobby is an agent, not a chatbot. It reads the account, does the research, proposes a trade with a reason, and once I confirm it places the order itself through the linked RockFlow account. It also remembers how I like to trade between sessions. The rule for this experiment: every morning I ask it what it would do with the account. It proposes, I confirm or refuse, and nothing goes out except through its chat.

Day 1, Sept 21, 10:59 ET. It proposed one share of AMZN with a limit at $256.05. I said yes. Filled at $255.73, fee $1.40. That's the whole day.

One share is deliberately small. The point for now is whether its reasons hold up over weeks, not the P&L. Two things I'm watching: whether it ever tells me to sell, and whether it changes behaviour after I tell it what I don't want.

One mistake already baked in: I didn't save its reasoning for this trade, and you'll see I didn't for the next few either. From the live part of the log onward every suggestion gets pasted into a file before I act.

Day 1 question for people who've run something like this: how small is too small to learn anything? One share feels like a demo, not a test.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: you were asking where spend limits should live a couple of weeks ago, and confirm-every-order is the strictest answer there is. what I'd watch is day 30, when you're tapping confirm without reading the reason anymore.

replies.author: Accomplished_Fun_408
replies.body: Good memory, and yes, confirm-every-order is the strictest answer, which is exactly why it's the one I expect to decay first. You can already see it in Day 1: I confirmed without saving the reason. Two things against the day-30 rubber stamp: it has to state the one condition that would make the trade wrong, and I have to type a one-line reply to that before I confirm. No reply, no order. If I catch myself typing "ok" I'll say so in the log. How do you handle it on your side, a cap on approvals per day, or do you let the gateway carry the limit so the human can afford to get lazy?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: making the kill condition something you have to answer is what keeps the confirm from going free. I'd also count how many you clear in under ten seconds each week; when that climbs, it's a stamp again. I built Quantradin on the same split, the agent can close or pause by itself and opening anything waits for a human.

replies.author: Accomplished_Fun_408
replies.body: Time-to-confirm is a better tell than anything I had. From now on the log gets two timestamps per order, when it proposed and when I confirmed, and the weekly write-up reports the share cleared in under ten seconds. The open/close split is the one place I'd push back: in 18 days my worst decision was a close, selling three positions it had given me no reason to sell. On this account the closes are what need a human, and the opens are what it does well. Is your asymmetry about risk, a close can only reduce exposure, or about speed, a stop has to fire without waiting for me?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: fair, a close with no reason is still a decision and it can cost as much as an open. I'd hold closes to the same rule then: it states why, and only a stop it already had in place gets to skip that.
